title: A galloping horse does fly, but with its legs tucked in, not stretched out as painted

cover.alt: Muybridge’s 1878 silhouette photo of a jockey on a galloping mare in front of a lined white backdrop; all four hooves are off the ground, bunched beneath her body.

body: Most oil paintings of the 1870s showed a running horse in mid-air with its forelegs stretched forward and its hind legs back, like a flying squirrel. Leland Stanford, a horse breeder and former Governor of California, was convinced this was wrong and hired the photographer Eadweard Muybridge to prove it. In June 1878, at Stanford’s farm in Palo Alto, a battery of **12 cameras** caught the mare Sallie Gardner mid-stride. All four feet do leave the ground at once, but only when they are **gathered beneath the body**.

slides.alt: Muybridge’s 1878 photographs of the mare Sallie Gardner played in sequence as a loop: a jockey rides a dark horse at full gallop past a white backdrop with numbered lines.
slides.caption: Photographer Eadweard Muybridge’s 1878 photos of the mare Sallie Gardner, played in sequence. In the frames numbered 2 and 3, all four hooves are off the ground, tucked under her.

slides.prompt: In 1877 Muybridge sent newspapers an ‘instantaneous photograph’ of the trotter Occident. What was odd about it?
slides.answer: It was a photo of a painting
slides.detail: A retouch artist had painted it from Muybridge’s negative, with a cut-out photo of the driver’s face glued in place.

slides.question: Leland Stanford, who hired Muybridge, is often said to have bet a fortune on the photos. What does historian Phillip Prodger think?
slides.explanation: Prodger says there are no primary accounts of the bet ever taking place: everything is hearsay and secondhand information.
